steps.title: Controlling the order of your results with ORDER BY
steps.lede: A WHERE clause decides which orders come back, but not what order they appear in. ORDER BY gives you that control.

blocks.text: ORDER BY sorts result rows by the expression you name. If you don't specify a direction, ascending (ASC) order is assumed by default — so `ORDER BY delivery_time_minutes` lists the fastest QuickCart deliveries first. Add DESC to reverse it: `ORDER BY delivery_time_minutes DESC` puts the slowest deliveries at the top.

When two rows tie on the first sort expression, SQL compares them on the next one. `ORDER BY customer_id, delivery_time_minutes DESC` groups each customer's orders together (ascending by customer_id) and within each customer shows the slowest delivery first. You can chain as many tiebreaker columns as you need.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC

after.caption: After ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC

blocks.change_summary: Adding ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC groups rows by customer and within each customer shows the slowest delivery first.

steps.title: Using a second column as a tiebreaker
steps.lede: Test your understanding of how ORDER BY handles tied values.

public.prompt: A query ends with `ORDER BY region ASC, order_id DESC`. Two rows both have `region = 'south'`. How does SQL decide which of those two rows appears first?

options.text: The row with the larger `order_id` appears first, because the second expression sorts descending.
The row with the smaller `order_id` appears first, because ASC is the default for any tiebreaker.
SQL returns the two rows in the order they were inserted into the table.
SQL raises an error because two rows share the same value in the first sort column.

opt_a.message: Correct. When the first expression ties, SQL moves to the next expression. `order_id DESC` means the larger value comes first.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. The direction of the second expression is DESC, not ASC. DESC puts the larger value first.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. SQL does not guarantee storage order. The tiebreaker column — `order_id DESC` — determines the order.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. Ties on a sort column are not an error. SQL simply moves to the next ORDER BY expression to break the tie.

correct.message: Right. When the first sort column ties, SQL evaluates the next expression in the ORDER BY list. Here `order_id DESC` puts the higher order_id first.

incorrect.message: When two rows tie on the first sort column, SQL uses the next ORDER BY expression to break the tie. The direction of that expression (ASC or DESC) applies normally.

hints: Look at the second expression in the ORDER BY clause and its direction keyword.
DESC means the larger value comes first; ASC means the smaller value comes first.

subquery in FROM with an alias

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return order_id and region, sorted by region ASC then order_id DESC. Check your ORDER BY clause and column list.

correct.message: Your ORDER BY clause correctly sorts by region ascending and breaks ties with order_id descending. The rows appear in the exact order the two-column sort produces.

steps.title: Returning a slice of rows with LIMIT and OFFSET
steps.lede: Once results are sorted, LIMIT and OFFSET let you take just the rows you need — the top five, or the next page.

blocks.text: LIMIT restricts the maximum number of rows a query returns. OFFSET specifies how many rows to skip before returning rows. `SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders ORDER BY delivery_time_minutes DESC LIMIT 3` returns the three slowest deliveries in the QuickCart dataset.

When both are specified, OFFSET rows are skipped first, then up to LIMIT rows of what remains are returned. Adding `OFFSET 3` to that same query skips the three slowest and returns the next three — a second page of results.
Without ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET return an unpredictable subset. SQL promises no particular sequence unless ORDER BY is present.

blocks.title: How OFFSET and LIMIT slice a sorted result

nodes.label: OFFSET: skip first N rows
nodes.detail: e.g. OFFSET 3 discards the first 3 rows

blocks.alt_text: A sorted list passes through an OFFSET step that discards the first rows, then a LIMIT step that keeps the next rows, producing the final output.

steps.title: Predicting rows returned with LIMIT and OFFSET
steps.lede: Check that you can trace which rows OFFSET skips and LIMIT keeps.

public.prompt: A sorted query has 13 rows. You add `LIMIT 4 OFFSET 3`. Which rows does the result contain?

options.text: Rows 4, 5, 6, and 7 (the 4 rows after skipping the first 3).
Rows 1, 2, 3, and 4 (OFFSET is ignored when LIMIT is present).
Rows 3, 4, 5, and 6 (OFFSET skips rows starting from row 3).
Rows 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 (LIMIT 4 means skip 4, then return the next rows).

opt_a.message: Correct. OFFSET 3 skips the first 3 rows, leaving rows 4–13. LIMIT 4 then returns the next 4: rows 4, 5, 6, and 7.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. OFFSET is not ignored. When both are present, OFFSET rows are skipped first, then LIMIT rows are returned.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. OFFSET 3 skips rows 1, 2, and 3 entirely. The first returned row is row 4, not row 3.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. LIMIT 4 means return at most 4 rows, not skip 4. OFFSET 3 does the skipping.

correct.message: Exactly right. OFFSET 3 discards the first 3 rows, then LIMIT 4 takes the next 4, giving rows 4 through 7.

incorrect.message: Remember: OFFSET skips that many rows from the front of the sorted result, and LIMIT caps how many rows are returned after the skip.

hints: Think of OFFSET as 'how many rows to throw away before you start counting'.
After skipping OFFSET rows, LIMIT controls how many of the remaining rows you keep.

steps.title: Return the top 5 orders by amount
steps.lede: Write a query that returns the five highest-value orders from the orders table, sorted by amount descending.

public.prompt: The QuickCart team wants to see the five highest-value orders. Write a query that returns **order_id** and **amount** from the `orders` table, sorted by **amount descending**, and limited to exactly **5 rows**.

files.content:
-- orders columns: order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes, order_date, region, amount, city
-- Return order_id and amount.
-- Sort by amount from highest to lowest.
-- Return only the top 5 rows.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY amount DESC
LIMIT 5;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return order_id and amount for the 5 orders with the highest amount, in descending order. Check your ORDER BY direction and LIMIT clause.

correct.message: Your query correctly sorts by amount descending and uses LIMIT 5 to return only the top five orders.

incorrect.message: Make sure you sort by amount DESC (highest first) and add LIMIT 5 after the ORDER BY clause. Select only order_id and amount.

hints: To get the highest values first, use ORDER BY amount DESC.
LIMIT goes at the very end of the query, after ORDER BY.

steps.title: Sorting and limiting results
steps.lede: Two clauses that shape what comes back and in what order.

blocks.text: ORDER BY sorts result rows by one or more expressions. Omitting a direction defaults to ASC; add DESC to reverse. A second column in ORDER BY breaks ties on the first.
LIMIT caps the number of rows returned; OFFSET skips rows before the limit is applied. Always pair them with ORDER BY — without it the subset returned is unpredictable.

remediation_steps.title: How ORDER BY handles tied values
remediation_steps.lede: When two rows are equal on the first sort column, SQL moves to the next one.

blocks.text: If two rows are equal according to the leftmost ORDER BY expression, SQL compares them on the next expression. `ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC` first groups rows by customer_id; within each customer group, the row with the longest delivery time appears first. Without a second column, tied rows appear in an unspecified order.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (1,2) ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC

blocks.caption: Customers 1 and 2 sorted by customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC — ties on customer_id broken by delivery time

remediation_steps.title: OFFSET skips first, then LIMIT keeps
remediation_steps.lede: The two clauses work in sequence: skip, then keep.

blocks.text: When both OFFSET and LIMIT are present, OFFSET rows are skipped first, and then up to LIMIT rows of what remains are returned. On a 13-row orders table sorted by amount DESC: `LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3` skips the three highest-amount orders and returns the next three.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3

blocks.caption: LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3 on orders sorted by amount DESC — rows 4–6 of the sorted list
